summary: A near-verbatim copy of a white paper from the ESnet X.500/X.400 Task Force with recommendations for the first phase of deploying OSI Directory (X.500) and Message Handling (X.400) services in the ESnet research community. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A group of science network people write down a plan for starting up electronic phone books and mail services, so their sites can use them together.

subtitle: ESnet's guide to deploying global directory and mail services using OSI standards.

tldr.problem: The ESnet research community needed standardized, interoperable directory and email services so scientists could find each other and exchange messages reliably.
tldr.mechanism: ESnet's task force recommended deploying the OSI standards X.500 (for white pages directories) and X.400 (for message handling), providing both the services themselves and guidance for backbone sites.
tldr.outcome: This document served as a planning blueprint for Phase I deployment. X.500 and X.400 saw some adoption in research networks, though they were eventually superseded by DNS and SMTP/MIME.

today: This RFC is an informational document that recorded the Phase I deployment plans for X.500 and X.400 in the ESnet community in 1992. While X.500 and X.400 saw some adoption in research and government networks, they were eventually superseded in most of the Internet by DNS (for directory services) and SMTP/MIME (for email). However, X.500 concepts influenced later directory standards, and some government and telecom sectors continued to use these OSI protocols into later decades.

sections.title: Purpose and Context
sections.content:
This document is a near-verbatim republication of a white paper from the ESnet Site Coordinating Committee's X.500/X.400 Task Force. It recommends the initial deployment strategy for two major OSI (Open Systems Interconnection) protocols in the Energy Sciences Network: X.500 for directory services and X.400 for message handling. The Energy Sciences Network (ESnet) is a national US Department of Energy network supporting scientific research and remote access to major research facilities. At the time (1992), the community lacked a coordinated way to deploy these new standardized services, so the task force was created to establish a roadmap and ensure interoperability across ESnet's backbone sites.

The document addresses not only what services to deploy, but also naming conventions, security considerations, registration requirements, and the practical steps each ESnet site would need to follow. It is designed to give backbone sites a clear, coordinated approach so that services become mutually valuable across the entire ESnet community.
sections.plainLanguage: A team of network experts made a plan document explaining how to set up two new Internet services so all the science labs can use them together without confusion.

sections.title: X.500: Directory Services Explained
sections.content:
X.500 is a global directory standard that stores information about people, organizations, and other entities in a tree-like database called the Directory Information Tree (DIB). Think of it like a centralized, searchable phone book that many institutions contribute to and maintain. Each entry in X.500 is identified by a Distinguished Name (DN)—a path from the root of the tree down to the specific entry—ensuring every entry is uniquely named. For example, a person at Lawrence Livermore National Lab might be identified as c=US, o=Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory, cn=Allen Sturtevant.

X.500 stores white pages information such as names, postal addresses, telephone numbers, and email addresses (both SMTP and X.400 formats). Directory User Agents (DUAs) are client programs that let people search the directory, while Directory System Agents (DSAs) are servers that hold and distribute pieces of the directory tree. Users can access X.500 through multiple interfaces: interactive applications like POD and FRED, command-line tools like WHOIS and FINGER, or even email-based queries. ESnet recommended QUIPU, the publicly available X.500 implementation from University College London, to ensure interoperability across all participating sites.
sections.plainLanguage: X.500 is like a giant shared address book that many offices contribute to. You look people up by their organization and name, and it tells you their phone number and email address.

sections.title: X.400: Message Handling Services
sections.content:
X.400 is the OSI standard for electronic mail, defined by CCITT (now ITU) and adopted by ISO as part of MOTIS (Message-Oriented Text Interchange Systems). It uses a store-and-forward model where Message Transfer Agents (MTAs) relay messages through a distributed network. Messages consist of an envelope (routing and delivery information) and content (the message itself), and the content can carry multiple body parts in different formats: text, voice, facsimile, or other types. ESnet's Phase I deployment planned to establish a backbone of Private Management Domains (PRMDs)—one per ESnet backbone site—that would participate in ESnet's larger Administrative Management Domain (ADMD), providing X.400 mail service to the research community.

X.400 naming is hierarchical, with addresses structured like postal addresses: a country, organization, and local mailbox identifier. ESnet would establish naming conventions so that every site's X.400 address fit into a coordinated global structure. The service was intended to eventually integrate with X.500: X.500 directories could look up the X.400 address of a recipient, and X.400 could use X.500 for routing decisions, creating a tightly coupled services environment.
sections.plainLanguage: X.400 is an international mail system that lets organizations send mail to each other in a coordinated way. Each organization runs a mail server (an MTA) that knows how to deliver to other organizations' servers.

sections.title: Naming Structure and Registration
sections.content:
ESnet aligned with the PSI White Pages Pilot Project, the most established X.500 deployment in the United States. National laboratories and organizations with national standing are listed directly under c=US in the directory tree. Universities, commercial entities, and smaller organizations are placed under their state or city. For example, MIT appears under c=US, st=Massachusetts, o=MIT. Each ESnet backbone site becomes a Name Registration Authority responsible for administering all entries below its own organizational node, ensuring no duplicates and maintaining consistency within its sub-tree.

X.500 organization names must be nationally unique if they appear directly under c=US. ESnet recommended that organizations apply for ANSI (American National Standards Institute) alphanumeric nameform registration to confer national standing, or register with the GSA (General Services Administration) or US Patent and Trademark Office. Section 4 of the RFC details the registration procedures with each authority. Organizational unit names need only be unique relative to their parent node. To facilitate searching across the ESnet community as a whole, backbone sites are also listed as aliases under c=US, o=Energy Sciences Network, so users can find them in multiple places in the directory.
sections.plainLanguage: Everyone gets a unique name in the directory tree, like an address: country, state, organization, and local name. Each site administers its own part of the tree to make sure there are no duplicates.

sections.title: ESnet Services and Deployment Strategy
sections.content:
ESnet provided centralized services to help backbone sites join the X.500 and X.400 communities without having to operate their own servers immediately. ESnet operated Level-0 DSAs (the top-level directory servers for the c=US subtree) and would manage the X.500 information of any backbone site that did not yet wish to run its own DSA. Sites could submit their personnel data to ESnet in a simple ASCII format, and ESnet would update the shared directory monthly. To avoid administrative burden, ESnet enforced limits: at most one organization per site, up to 50 organizational units, 3 levels of hierarchy depth, and 5,000 person entries per site, with monthly update frequency.

For X.400, ESnet would establish an ESnet-wide backbone of MTAs that routed mail between participating sites. Each backbone site would operate its own PRMD (Private Management Domain) MTA, and ESnet provided an operations mailing list (x500-ops@es.net), a routing table published on the ESnet Information Server, and guidelines for PRMD registration and peering. ESnet also supported multiple protocol stacks—RFC-1006 over TCP/IP, TP4 over CLNP, and TP0 over X.25—to ensure that sites with different networking infrastructure could all interoperate. ESnet's DSAs and MTAs would act as relay points for sites that lacked direct connectivity, eliminating the risk that a site would receive a referral to another DSA or MTA it could not reach.
sections.plainLanguage: ESnet runs central servers that help sites participate without having to run their own, updating the directory monthly with each site's contact information. ESnet also acts as a mail hub, making sure mail can reach every site no matter what network equipment they use.

sections.title: Future Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC acknowledges several open issues that would need attention in later phases. One major question was how Administrative Directory Management Domains (ADDMDs)—commercial or government-operated directory services—would interoperate with private PRDMDs. Another was the closer integration of X.400 and X.500: at the time, the two systems did not fully leverage each other, but future versions of both standards and implementations were expected to allow X.500 to look up recipient information and routing paths for X.400 messages in a fully integrated manner. The RFC also noted that commercial X.500 implementations were emerging; QUIPU, while interoperable, might not meet all needs in future deployments. A final consideration was the interaction between X.500 and DECdns, Digital Equipment Corporation's namespace system, which was evolving at the same time and might eventually interoperate with X.500 through new versions of the Digital networking stack.

The document emphasizes that X.500 and X.400 are continuously evolving standards, updated every four years by CCITT/ITU and every two years in the US GOSIP (Government OSI Profile) profile. What this RFC defines as Phase I was understood to be just the beginning; successive phases would add richer functionality, support for more content types, broader interoperability, and integration with emerging commercial services and competing standards.
sections.plainLanguage: The plan recognizes that directory and mail systems will keep changing. In the future, commercial services might join in, the two systems might work better together, and different vendors' products might need to cooperate more smoothly.
